rationale: Requested execution of the four-order probe on a two-carrier/two-empty reply set, which separates the first delivered reply from the reply adopted at the slow-quorum trigger. The question's discriminator asked both whether the remaining permutations of the three-reply set behave as the trigger position predicts and whether a reply set with more command-carrying than empty replies flips the outcome; this reply set keeps the deciding position fixed at the second delivered reply while varying which kind of reply occupies it, and it observes the trigger directly by noting when the recoverer's leader bookkeeping object is replaced, instead of deriving the trigger position from the configuration.

scope.description: Owner replica 0 proposes X on its own instance (0,0) and replica 1's non-equal pre-accept reply is delivered, so the owner enters the Accept phase at ballot 0 towards replicas 1 and 2; both accept, replica 1 with status PREACCEPTED and replica 2 with status PREACCEPTED_EQ, while replicas 3 and 4 hold the instance with no command. The owner's AcceptReplies are left in flight. The owner, alive and still holding X, then runs startRecoveryForInstance(0,0) and its own PrepareReply (carrying X at status ACCEPTED) joins the reply set, so the adoption loop sees up to five elements: the recoverer's own reply plus the four peers' answers, two of which carry X and two of which carry no command at the same value ballot 0. The harness collects each recipient's messages, then delivers the four peer replies in a declared order, re-reading the recoverer's leader bookkeeping pointer after every delivery. The test runs the same message set in four orders: 1,2,3,4 (first and trigger reply carry the command); 1,3,4,2 (first carries it, trigger reply does not); 3,4,1,2 (neither the first nor the trigger reply carries it); 3,1,4,2 (the first reply carries nothing while the trigger reply carries the command). Each run records the delivered order, the per-delivery bookkeeping state, the delivery at which the bookkeeping object is replaced (the trigger), whether that delivery's reply carried the command, and what the instance holds afterwards.
assumptions: Same construction, transport boundary and crash model as the other experiments in this harness.
Delivery order among the prepare replies is chosen by the harness, which is what a real network does not fix; the read order is not altered.

No production logic is modified; the trigger is detected only by comparing the recoverer's own leader-bookkeeping pointer across a delivery, which the target's dispatch replaces when it hands the instance to startPhase1.

The reply set is fixed across the four runs: the recoverer's own reply plus two command-carrying and two empty peer replies, all at value ballot 0, so the number of command-carrying replies exceeds the number of empty peer replies that can be delivered before the trigger.
excluded: No client path, no state-machine execution, no run() loop or recovery timer loop.
No order in which the empty replies outnumber all command-carrying elements, which this configuration cannot produce because the accept wave covers two peers only.

experiment.prefix: The harness drives the owner's proposal and accept phase through the target's own handlers, delivers the Accept to replicas 1 and 2, then calls the owner's startRecoveryForInstance(0,0). Each peer's messages are collected before delivery; the harness then delivers them one recipient at a time in the declared order, reading the owner's leader bookkeeping before and after each delivery and emitting the full bookkeeping state (prepared flag, ballot, status, candidate command length, appended reply count) after every delivery, plus a dedicated event on the delivery whose bookkeeping pointer changed. After the deliveries it drains the owner's own follow-up messages and records the instance's status, command length and the command length of any PreAccept the owner emitted.
experiment.requirement: A recovery of an instance must not drop the instance's command when a reply without a command arrives at the same value ballot as replies that carry one, and the adopted value must not depend on the delivery order of equally admissible replies.
experiment.responsibility: The recovering replica's own adoption loop and sub-case dispatch (epaxos/epaxos.go:1236-1313): the replies are the acceptors' and the recoverer's own honests answers at their stored ballots, and the harness only chooses the arrival order.

comparisons.description: Run A (replies 1,2,3,4): both the first delivered reply and the reply adopted at the trigger carry the command, so the instance is expected to keep the owner's command.

Run D (replies 1,3,4,2): the first delivered reply carries the command while the reply adopted at the trigger does not, so a violated outcome shows the loss does not require an empty reply to arrive first and that a command-carrying element present when the trigger fires does not protect the command.

Run B (replies 3,4,1,2): neither the first delivered reply nor the trigger reply carries the command, so the two command-carrying replies arrive after the trigger; a violated outcome shows replies delivered after the trigger cannot restore the command even though they outnumber the empty replies already adopted.

Run C (replies 3,1,4,2): the first delivered reply carries nothing while the trigger reply carries the command, so the expected outcome is that the instance keeps the owner's command; together with run D this separates which reply is delivered first from which reply is adopted at the trigger.

experiment.revision_reason: Replaced the previous mixed-order probe with a four-order probe over the same two-carrier/two-empty reply set and made the trigger observable: the harness now reads the recoverer's leader-bookkeeping pointer before and after each delivery and emits a trigger event when the dispatch replaces it, emits the bookkeeping and instance state after every delivery, and records which reply occupied the trigger position and whether it carried the command. The earlier derived field second_reply_carries_command compared the first command-carrying reply with the second delivered reply and is replaced by the recorded trigger reply and its command state. Scenario, handlers and the compared outcome field are unchanged.
